newsitem.title: UK: Police ring Catholic church as Protestants gather.
newsitem.headline: Police ring Catholic church as Protestants gather.

text.p: Hundreds of police ringed a Catholic church in Ballymena on Saturday night to smother a potential flashpoint protest by Protestants on the eve of the first anniversary of the IRA ending its 17 month truce.

Dozens of armoured police jeeps blocked streets around the church at Harryville, a suburb of Ballymena, to prevent trouble erupting when Protestants marched on the church, which has been the centre of a 23-week protest.
Several hundred Catholics attended a Saturday evening mass and left quickly before a planned Protestant march outside their place of worship later in the evening.
The protest underlined deep divisions in Northern Ireland society almost a year after Catholic-backed Irish Republican Army guerrillas ended a 17-month truce and dashed hopes of a peace settlement.

Father Eammon Cowan told the congregation to pray for hundreds of Protestants massed behind police lines in nearby streets. "Hatred is a demon. Pray for those afflicted by hatred," he told the congregation.
Protestants have picketed the church for 23 weeks to protest at the refusal of Catholics in the nearby village of Dunloy to allow a Protestant Orange Order parade last summer.
Community leaders had agreed to postpone the parade until the evening mass ended to avoid confrontation with worshippers.
Ian Paisley and other members of the Protestant Unionist movement, which want the province to stay British, have condemned the protest and say all religious faith must be respected.

The protest has underlined tension between Northern Ireland's 40 percent Irish Catholic minority, which sympathises with efforts to reunite the province with Ireland, and the Protestant majority which wants it to remain British.

It is also viewed by security officials as a bad omen for the yearly Protestant marching season, a flashpoint period which starts officially on March 31 and which last year provoked the worst civil strife in the province for decades.

Last July police first banned, then allowed, a Protestant Orange Order parade in the southern town of Portadown after Protestant protests across the province. The decision unleashed a wave of Catholic anger and polarised the already divided province.
Saturday night's parade was being staged almost a year after the February 9 bombing of London's Canary Wharf business complex by the IRA.

The IRA, which seeks to end British rule, has bombed security targets in Northern Ireland several times every week this year to back its demand that its political wing, Sinn Fein, be invited to Belfast peace talks.
